bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Hourly Rate and the Sydney Average Salary

If you’re paid by the hour or considering a salary offer, converting between hourly and annual figures helps you compare your earnings with benchmarks like the **Sydney average salary**. This guide walks you through the standard 38‑hour week, fortnightly pay, tax, and superannuation using the latest official figures.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly × Hours × 52

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For a full‑time employee working 38 hours each week, the multiplier is 1,976 (38 × 52). This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. It’s a starting point for comparison.

For example, if your hourly rate is $30.00:
- Weekly pay: $30.00 × 38 = $1,140.00
- Fortnightly pay: $1,140.00 × 2 = $2,280.00
- Annual gross: $30.00 × 38 × 52 = $59,280.00

You can use [the timesheet](/) to enter your base hourly rate and see these figures instantly. A checkbox adds 25% casual loading on top – never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

### The Sydney Average Salary and National Benchmarks

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reports Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) for full‑time adult ordinary time as $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). That equates to an annual salary of about $108,352.40. For all employees (including part‑time), total average weekly earnings are $1,579.20, or roughly $82,118.40 per year. While these are national figures, the **Sydney average salary** may differ due to industry mix and cost of living. The ABS does not publish a separate Sydney average, but you can compare your converted annual figure to these national benchmarks to gauge where you sit.

### Minimum Wage, Awards, and Casual Loading

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees receive at least $33.05 per hour, which includes the 25% casual loading. Many employees are covered by award rates that are higher than the minimum. Always check your industry award via [pay guides](/blog) or the Fair Work Ombudsman website.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026) up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. It is not deducted from your hourly rate. For a casual worker on $33.05 per hour (including loading), the employer still pays 12% super on the ordinary time component (the base rate before loading).

### Tax on Your Annual Pay

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your tax using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income over $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed in this estimate). This estimate does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool for a more detailed calculation.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many employers pay fortnightly. Your fortnightly gross is simply weekly pay × 2. For a $30/hour rate on 38 hours, that’s $2,280.00 before tax. After tax and Medicare, your take‑home will be lower – see the [reference tables](/data) for approximate tax withheld.

### Putting It All Together

To compare your earnings with the **Sydney average salary**, start with your hourly rate. Multiply by 38 (if full‑time) and by 52 to get annual gross. Then deduct estimated tax and Medicare to see your net income. Remember that super is additional – it’s not part of your take‑home pay but builds your retirement savings.

For award‑free employees, the National Minimum Wage is the floor. If you’re casual, ensure you’re receiving the 25% loading on top of the base rate. The [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how this works.

Finally, keep in mind that your actual pay may vary if you work different hours, receive penalties, or have salary packaging. This guide provides a standard conversion – always consult your employer or a professional for your specific situation.
